opus-5.5.text:
I think the two goals are much more aligned than people assume. If you want AI to keep advancing quickly, the biggest threat to that isn't safety researchers; it's a major disaster. Look at nuclear power. After Three Mile Island and Chernobyl, the backlash and regulation basically froze the industry for decades in many countries. We lost a lot of the potential benefit of clean energy because the risks weren't managed well up front, and then the public and policymakers overcorrected.

AI could go the same way. If there's a serious incident, say a model meaningfully helps someone carry out a bioweapons attack, or there's a large-scale cyberattack on critical infrastructure, you'd probably get a very blunt, heavy-handed response. That kind of reaction tends to be much more restrictive than thoughtful risk management would have been beforehand.

So even if your only goal is acceleration, you should want the tail risks handled, because one catastrophe can set the whole field back. Good risk management keeps the road open. It's like brakes on a car: they're what let you drive fast with confidence, not what slows you down.

There's also a reliability point. Systems people can trust get deployed more widely. If businesses, governments and the public believe these systems are robust, controllable and not easily misused, adoption goes up. Safety and capability aren't purely a tradeoff. A lot of safety work is about making systems work as intended, which is part of making them useful.

And finally, the stakes are lopsided. Some risks, like losing control of very capable systems or enabling mass-casualty weapons, are irreversible. You can always speed up later if you've been too careful in some area, but you can't undo a catastrophe. Even someone very optimistic about AI's upside should want to protect that upside, and managing the downside is how you do it.

r001.rationale: It says a serious AI incident could trigger a restrictive response and set the field back, substantially slowing further development.

r002.rationale: The response discusses nuclear power, not aviation disasters or persistent fear of flying.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss aviation regulation or whether it arose reactively after disasters.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the framing that these are opposed, because historically the technologies that scaled fastest were the ones where people got the safety story right early. Think about aviation. Nobody flies because planes are fast; people fly because planes are fast and they almost never fall out of the sky. The safety engineering is what unlocked the mass adoption. Nuclear power is the counterexample. A couple of high-profile accidents and public trust collapsed, regulation got extremely heavy-handed, and the whole field basically stagnated for decades. If you're an accelerationist, that's the scenario you should be terrified of. One bad enough incident, something involving a bioweapon or a major cyberattack where AI was clearly instrumental, and you don't get careful policy, you get a panicked overreaction that sets the field back enormously.

So the first reason is just self-interest. Risk management is how you protect your license to operate.

The second thing I'd say is that the kind of risk management I care about is pretty mundane. It's not "pause everything." It's things like: have a safety culture where people can raise concerns without being punished, do red-teaming before you deploy, have compute and model-weight security so a frontier model doesn't just get stolen by a state actor, and have some minimal legal accountability so that the incentives aren't purely "ship it and externalize the downside." None of that is anti-progress. That's just what a mature industry looks like.

And the third point is about where the real risks come from. A lot of the accelerationist crowd imagines the danger as sci-fi, a rogue AI waking up, and so they dismiss it. But if you look at the structural picture, the biggest risks are things like competitive pressure, where everyone races and cuts corners because they're afraid of being second, or malicious use, where the same capabilities that help a biologist help someone trying to engineer a pathogen. Those are problems with the ecosystem and the incentives, not some mystical property of the model. You can't engineer your way out of a bad race dynamic by just building faster. You actually need coordination, standards, some amount of governance.

So I'd say if you genuinely want transformative AI to arrive and to go well, and to be allowed to go well, you should want the people building it to be competent at managing risk. The alternative isn't faster progress. The alternative is a disaster that makes everyone slow down whether they want to or not.

r001.rationale: It says a major AI-enabled incident could trigger a panicked overreaction that sets the field back enormously and make everyone slow down.

r002.rationale: The aviation example says safety enabled mass adoption; it does not suggest that disasters contribute to persistent public fear of flying.

r003.rationale: It does not say aviation regulation emerged in response to disasters or contrast reactive regulation with proactive prevention.

astra-6.text:
If you want AI development to accelerate, you should care about keeping that progress sustainable. A major catastrophe could trigger a public backlash and sweeping restrictions, including restrictions on applications that are genuinely beneficial. Ignoring risks can therefore undermine the very progress you’re trying to promote.

Think about brakes on a car. They don’t just let you stop; they let you travel faster with confidence. In the same way, good evaluations, security, and safeguards can make it possible to deploy more capable systems responsibly. The question shouldn’t be whether we choose progress or safety. It should be which risk-management measures let us capture the benefits of AI while reducing the chances of something that would derail them.

r001.rationale: It says a major catastrophe could trigger public backlash and sweeping restrictions, undermining progress, clearly conveying that catastrophe could substantially slow later AI development.

r002.rationale: The response contains no mention of aviation disasters or persistent public fear of flying.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss aviation regulation or whether it emerged reactively after disasters.

sol-6.1.text:
If you want AI development to keep accelerating, you should care about the things that could derail it. A major incident could destroy public trust, trigger a backlash, and lead to very broad restrictions. So even from a strongly pro-progress perspective, it makes sense to invest in safety and security early.

Think about cybersecurity. You don’t help a company move faster over the long run by ignoring security until it gets hacked. You build the infrastructure that lets it operate reliably. AI risk management plays a similar role: evaluate what systems can do, understand where they fail, and put safeguards around dangerous capabilities.

There are also risks that come from other actors. You might trust your own intentions, but that doesn’t mean you want everyone to have unrestricted access to capabilities that could cause enormous harm. Managing those risks helps preserve the benefits of AI and the conditions under which development can continue. Progress and risk management can reinforce each other.

r001.rationale: It says a major AI incident could trigger a backlash and very broad restrictions, derailing continued development.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention aviation disasters or persistent public fear of flying.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss aviation regulation or whether it arose reactively after disasters.
